newsitem.title: USA: Judge's ruling sends Mass. Democrats scrambling.
newsitem.headline: Judge's ruling sends Mass. Democrats scrambling.

text.p: The most hotly contested race in Massachusetts is no longer the battle between incumbent Democrat Sen. John Kerry and Republican Gov. William Weld, but an unexpected internal Democratic war to challenge for retiring Congressman Gerry Studds' seat.

In a stunning reversal on Friday, a Massachusetts judge declared William Delahunt the winner of the Sept. 17 Democratic primary in the 10th district. The ruling was handed down even as Philip Johnston, the apparent winner, was on a campaign stop with first lady Hillary Clinton.

Johnston, 52, a liberal and former state representative who lacked funds for a television campaign in the primary, was initially declared the winner by a 206 vote margin. After a recount in selected districts certified by the Secretary of State William Galvin, his lead had shrunk to 175.

But Norfolk Superior Court Judge Elizabeth Donovan ruled, after a review of more than 900 challenged ballots, that Delahunt, the Norfolk district attorney, actually won the race by 108 votes. She ordered Galvin to print new ballots with Delahunt's name.
A spokesman for Galvin said on Saturday the printer had been alerted.
The disputed ballot papers were punch-card ballots, which in many cases were marked for Delahunt but read by an electronic scanner as blanks because they were not punched clean through, Galvin said.

After his court victory, Delahunt told reporters, "I need every Democrat, every independent and a good chunk of Republicans to make this seat the kind of seat that would be a fitting legacy to Gerry Studds."
But with only a month left to the election, it is unclear if Delahunt will get his wish.

Johnston told reporters he would go to the state's highest court, the Supreme Judicial Court, on Monday seeking an expedited hearing, and in the meantime, ask them to order ballots with both names printed.
He promised, "a very agressive court fight" for the district that covers Cape Cod and the south shore of Massachusetts Bay.
State Democrats note that with just 30 days left until the election, the clear winner in this battle is Republican candidate Edward Teague.

The Delahunt-Johnston fight is causing confusion among voters, according to Quincy City Councillor Paul Harold, who called the ruling "a setback ... we have to keep a Democratic congressman in this district if we expect to turn over the majority in Washington."
Teague, who began airing attack advertisments on Johnston this week, said it made little difference which man he faced.
"There's no difference between these candidates in terms of their opinions on critical issues," Teague told reporters.
